clinicalPearls: Periodontitis is a biofilm-driven inflammatory disease causing irreversible destruction of the periodontal attachment and alveolar bone
The hallmark distinguishing it from gingivitis is loss of clinical attachment and true periodontal pocketing, not just bleeding gums
It is often painless and slowly progressive, so patients may present late with mobility, drifting teeth, or gingival recession
Probing depths, attachment levels, bleeding on probing, and radiographic bone loss are the core diagnostic measurements
Smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, and genetic susceptibility strongly modify disease severity and treatment response
There is a bidirectional relationship with diabetes and associations with cardiovascular and other systemic conditions
Treatment centres on meticulous plaque control and mechanical debridement to disrupt the subgingival biofilm, with surgery for residual defects
Long-term supportive periodontal maintenance is essential because the disease tends to recur without ongoing care
reference.pathophysiology: Periodontitis arises from a dysbiotic subgingival biofilm dominated by anaerobic and gram-negative species that provoke a chronic host immune-inflammatory response. Bacterial virulence factors and the resulting inflammatory mediators drive activation of osteoclasts and matrix-degrading enzymes, leading to breakdown of the periodontal ligament and resorption of alveolar bone. This produces apical migration of the junctional epithelium and true pocket formation. The extent of tissue destruction reflects the balance between microbial challenge and host response, which is heavily modulated by risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, and genetics, ultimately threatening tooth support.
additionalDifferentials: Manifestations of systemic disease affecting the periodontium
additionalInvestigations: Full-mouth periodontal charting of probing depths and attachment loss
Bleeding on probing and plaque indices
Periapical and bitewing radiographs to assess bone loss
Assessment of tooth mobility and furcation involvement
Screening for diabetes and smoking status as risk modifiers
redFlags: Rapid attachment and bone loss in a young patient suggesting aggressive disease
Necrotising periodontitis with pain, ulceration, and tissue destruction, especially in immunocompromised patients
Periodontal manifestations pointing to undiagnosed diabetes or immune deficiency
reference.prognosis: With effective plaque control and professional care, disease progression can usually be halted and teeth retained, but lost attachment and bone do not regenerate spontaneously and advanced cases carry a guarded prognosis for affected teeth.
pitfalls: Treating bleeding gums as simple gingivitis while missing established attachment loss
Neglecting smoking cessation and glycaemic control that undermine treatment
Relying on antibiotics instead of mechanical biofilm disruption
Failing to arrange ongoing maintenance, allowing recurrence
management: Achieve effective biofilm control through oral hygiene instruction and daily mechanical plaque removal by the patient
Perform subgingival instrumentation (scaling and root surface debridement) as the cornerstone of non-surgical therapy
Use adjunctive antimicrobials selectively, such as antiseptic mouthrinses or systemic antibiotics in aggressive or refractory disease
Modify risk factors by supporting smoking cessation and optimising glycaemic control in diabetes, given the bidirectional relationship
Offer periodontal surgery (flap, resective or regenerative procedures) for residual deep pockets and furcation involvement
Enrol patients in structured supportive periodontal maintenance with regular monitoring of probing depths, attachment levels and bleeding on probing
Extract teeth of hopeless prognosis and plan prosthetic replacement
